```{r, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", fig.width = 6, fig.height = 4.5,
                      eval = requireNamespace("ggplot2", quietly = TRUE))
```

The simulations of comdynamite can be turned around: instead of asking what patterns a set of
processes produces, we can ask which values of the parameters of a process make simulated
metacommunities look like an observed one. Approximate Bayesian computation (ABC) does this by
simulating many data sets with parameters drawn from a prior, describing each with summary
statistics, and keeping the parameters whose statistics resemble the observed ones. With random
forests (Pudlo et al. 2016; Raynal et al. 2019), there is no tolerance or distance to choose: a
forest learns how the parameters relate to the statistics in the reference table and weighs its
rows by their similarity to the observed data.

This vignette goes through the whole workflow with the anurans of 40 urban ponds in two
Brazilian cities (`anurans`):

1. build a landscape from the coordinates of the ponds and write the simulator;
2. simulate a reference table with `abc_table()`;
3. check that the parameters can be recovered at all, with `abc_recovery()`;
4. choose between models with `abc_choose()`;
5. estimate the parameters for the observed data with `abc_fit()`, and check the fit with
   `abc_diagnose()`, `abc_ppc()` and cross-validation over spatial blocks with `abc_cv()`.

The reference tables (about 20,000 simulations) take about a quarter of an hour on six cores,
and they and the forests were computed in advance with
[`data-raw/abc_anurans.R`](https://github.com/diogoprov/comdynamite/blob/main/data-raw/abc_anurans.R);
the rest runs here.

```{r setup}
library(comdynamite)
library(ggplot2)
res <- readRDS("abc.rds")
```

## The data and the simulator

The ponds of each city are a few kilometres apart, and the two cities are about 900 km from each
other, so we treat them as two metacommunities that share the values of the parameters. Each pond
has a hydrology score, from small, shallow and warm ponds (0) to large and deep ones (100), and
the urban cover within 1 km. Each city has its own regional pool: the anurans that breed in
lentic water and were recorded by GBIF in its ecoregion and within 200 km of its ponds (see
`?anurans`). The pools are much larger than the sets of species found in the ponds, so the
simulations must explain which species of the region reach and persist in the ponds.

```{r data}
table(anurans$city)
c(recorded = ncol(anurans$comm), pool = ncol(anurans$pool))
tapply(rowSums(anurans$pool), anurans$city, max)
city <- ifelse(anurans$city == "Campo Grande", "cg", "sjc")
pool <- anurans$pool
rownames(pool) <- paste0("site", seq_along(city))
```

`landscape_points()` keeps the real layout of the ponds. With `lonlat = TRUE`, distances are
great-circle distances in kilometres, and `disp_scale` is the scale of the exponential dispersal
kernel in kilometres.

```{r landscape}
ponds <- landscape_points(anurans$coords, anurans$env[, "hydrology"], disp_scale = 2,
                          lonlat = TRUE)
ponds
```

The model has six parameters: the fraction of individuals that emigrate at each step
(`log_dispersal`, on a log10 scale), the scale of the dispersal kernel (`log_kernel`, log10 km),
the strength of competition between the most closely related species (`inter_max`, with
competition decreasing with phylogenetic distance), the mean niche breadth along the hydrology
axis (`sigma_mean`), the phylogenetic signal of the niche optima (`lambda`, Pagel's lambda), and
the share of species that tolerate any urban cover (`q_tol`). Following the chapter from which
the data come, each of the other species gets a threshold drawn from U(0, 100)% and is kept out
of ponds whose urban cover exceeds it; the filter acts on the pool of each pond, before the
dynamics. The simulator takes one draw of the parameters (`scenario`) and the objects shared by
all simulations (`shared`):

```{r simulator}
shared <- list(tree = anurans$tree, coords = anurans$coords, env = anurans$env[, "hydrology"],
               urban = anurans$env[, "urban_cover"], pool = pool, city = city)
prior <- list(log_dispersal = c(-4, log10(0.3)), log_kernel = log10(c(0.5, 20)),
              inter_max = c(0, 1), sigma_mean = c(5, 100), lambda = c(0, 1), q_tol = c(0, 1))
urban_pool <- function(pool, urban, q_tol) {
  threshold <- ifelse(runif(ncol(pool)) < q_tol, Inf, runif(ncol(pool), 0, 100))
  filtered <- pool * outer(urban, threshold, "<=")
  lost <- colSums(filtered) == 0  # a species excluded everywhere keeps its pool
  filtered[, lost] <- pool[, lost]
  filtered
}
simulate <- function(scenario, shared) {
  landscape <- landscape_points(shared$coords, shared$env, 10^scenario$log_kernel, lonlat = TRUE)
  simulate_metacommunity(landscape,
                         species_traits(shared$tree, scenario$lambda,
                                        sigma_mean = scenario$sigma_mean,
                                        sigma_sd = scenario$sigma_mean / 2),
                         competition_matrix(shared$tree, "phylo",
                                            inter_max = scenario$inter_max),
                         dispersal = 10^scenario$log_dispersal, n_steps = 500,
                         pool = urban_pool(shared$pool, shared$urban, scenario$q_tol))
}
set.seed(1)
sim <- simulate(list(log_dispersal = -2, log_kernel = 0.3, inter_max = 0.5, sigma_mean = 20,
                     lambda = 0.5, q_tol = 0.3), shared)
rowSums(sim$abundance > 0)[1:10]
```

## Summary statistics

The observed data are counts from surveys, whose totals depend on effort and on how easily each
species is detected, so we describe both the observed and the simulated metacommunities by
incidence alone: the statistics of `summary_stats()` that need no abundances (mean and total
richness, beta diversity, occupancy, the standardised effect sizes of MPD and MNTD, and distance
decay), plus the correlations of richness and of compositional dissimilarity with hydrology.
They are computed separately for each city, with the prefixes `cg_` and `sjc_`, over the
species of its regional pool, which is also the pool of the null model of the standardised
effect sizes. See `data-raw/abc_anurans.R` for the function; the observed statistics are

```{r observed}
round(res$observed[grepl("^(cg|sjc)_", names(res$observed))], 3)
```

With the simulator and the statistics in hand, `abc_table()` draws parameters uniformly from the
prior and runs one simulation per draw, in parallel with future:

```{r table, eval = FALSE}
future::plan(future::multicore, workers = 6)
table <- abc_table(prior, simulate, n = 10200, setup = function() shared,
                   summarise = summarise, seed = 2040)
```

## Can the parameters be recovered?

Before looking at the observed data, we ask whether the statistics carry information about
each parameter. `abc_recovery()` leaves `r res$settings$n_test` simulations out of the
reference table, treats each as if it were observed, and compares the estimates with the true
values. A parameter is worth estimating when the estimates follow the truth (R² well above
zero) and the 90% intervals contain the truth about 90% of the time.

```{r recovery}
print(res$recovery, digits = 2)
```

```{r recovery-plot, fig.alt = "Estimated against true values of the five parameters for the pseudo-observations, with the line of equality."}
ggplot(res$estimates, aes(truth, estimate)) +
  geom_abline(colour = "grey60") +
  geom_point(size = 0.8, alpha = 0.6) +
  facet_wrap(~parameter, scales = "free") +
  labs(x = "True value", y = "Posterior median") +
  theme_minimal()
```

Competition (`inter_max`) and emigration are well recovered, and niche breadth and tolerance to
urban cover reasonably so, while the scale of the kernel is only weakly identified and the
phylogenetic signal of the niche (`lambda`) not at all: with incidence in 40 ponds, its
posterior will be its prior. The intervals have about the right coverage for all six, so the
posterior of `lambda` is honest about this, just uninformative.

## Which model?

The same statistics may come from metacommunities without competition. We simulated a second
table with `inter_max` fixed at zero (the other five parameters from the same priors) and let
`abc_choose()` tell the two models apart:

```{r choice}
res$choice$error
res$choice$confusion
print(res$chosen, digits = 2)
```

The out-of-bag error shows that the two models are easy to tell apart when one of them is true.
For the observed data, `r res$chosen$votes_phylogenetic` of the 500 trees vote for the model
with phylogenetic competition, and the posterior probability of that model is
`r round(res$chosen$probability, 2)`.

## The posterior

`abc_fit()` grows one regression forest per parameter, and `predict()` gives the posterior
median and a 90% interval for the observed statistics:

```{r posterior}
print(res$posterior, digits = 2)
```

The rows of the reference table that the forests weigh give an approximate sample from the
posterior, which we can set against the uniform prior:

```{r posterior-plot, fig.alt = "Histograms of posterior draws of the five parameters, with the prior range shown by the horizontal extent of each panel."}
draws <- stack(res$draws[names(res$prior)])
limits <- data.frame(ind = names(res$prior), low = sapply(res$prior, `[`, 1),
                     high = sapply(res$prior, `[`, 2))
ggplot(draws, aes(values)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 25, fill = "grey40") +
  geom_blank(aes(x = low), limits) + geom_blank(aes(x = high), limits) +
  facet_wrap(~ind, scales = "free") +
  labs(x = "Value (panel width = prior range)", y = "Draws") +
  theme_minimal()
```

These draws use the mean of the weights of the six forests, so they are broader than the
intervals of each parameter.

## Checking the fit

A posterior is only as good as the model behind it. `abc_diagnose()` asks whether the observed
statistics lie within the range of the reference table and how many rows carry the weight
(effective sample size, ESS):

```{r diagnose}
print(res$diagnose, digits = 2)
```

A posterior predictive check compares the observed statistics with those of the simulations
drawn from the posterior. It is most telling for statistics left out of the fit, so we fitted a
second set of forests without the phylogenetic statistics and checked those:

```{r ppc}
print(res$ppc_phylo, digits = 2)
```

```{r ppc-values, include = FALSE}
pp <- function(x, stat) round(x$p[x$statistic == stat], 3)
im <- function(p) p[p$parameter == "inter_max", ]
```

The model chosen with a posterior probability of `r round(res$chosen$probability, 2)` fails
here. With competition among close relatives, the simulated ponds hold species more distantly
related than expected from the regional pool (standardised MPD above zero), whereas in the
observed ponds the species are as related as, or more related than, random draws from the pool.
The observed MPD is in the lower tail in both cities (p = `r pp(res$ppc_phylo, "cg_ses_mpd")` in
Campo Grande and `r pp(res$ppc_phylo, "sjc_ses_mpd")` in São José dos Campos). With all the
statistics in the fit, the forests pull the posterior towards the observed MPD and the misfit
is milder:

```{r ppc-all}
print(res$ppc_all[c("statistic", "observed", "median", "low", "high", "p")], digits = 2)
```

Why, then, does model choice favour competition so strongly? The statistics that weigh most in
the forest of `inter_max` are the mean and total richness of each city:

```{r importance}
head(res$importance[res$importance$parameter == "inter_max", ], 4)
```

With pools of 50 to 150 species, the observed ponds hold few of them, and among the processes in
the simulator, competition is the one that can keep richness that low. Any process that limits
richness but is missing from the model, such as colonisation from a region where most species
are rare, may therefore be read as competition. The phylogenetic statistics, which measure who
coexists rather than how many, seem to point instead to a filter that favours some clades, for
instance a tolerance to urban cover shared by related species, whereas the filter of the
simulator acts at random with respect to phylogeny. These are hypotheses for a better model,
not conclusions: the check says what the model misses, not why.

Leaving out total richness and beta diversity (total over mean richness) changes little, so the
choice does not rest on them alone:

```{r reduced}
print(res$reduced$chosen, digits = 2)
print(res$reduced$posterior, digits = 2)
```

## Cross-validation over space

The last check asks whether the model fitted to some ponds predicts the others. With spatial
blocks, the ponds left out are not neighbours of those kept (Roberts et al. 2017). We split each
city into two blocks with `spatial_folds()`, so that each of the four folds leaves out half of
one city, and `fold_summarise()` computed the statistics of the ponds kept and of those left out
in every simulation:

```{r folds, fig.alt = "Ponds of the two cities coloured by fold."}
ggplot(data.frame(anurans$coords, fold = factor(res$folds), city = anurans$city),
       aes(lon, lat, colour = fold)) +
  geom_point() +
  facet_wrap(~city, scales = "free") +
  theme_minimal()
```

`abc_cv()` fits the forests on the statistics of the ponds kept and predicts those of the ponds
left out. `summary()` gives, for each statistic, the fraction of folds in which the observed
value fell inside the 90% predictive interval:

```{r cv}
print(res$cv_summary, digits = 2)
```

With only four folds, these fractions are coarse, but most statistics of the ponds left out are
predicted. The exceptions repeat the posterior predictive check: the standardised MPD of the
ponds left out falls below the prediction in most folds, so the misfit is not confined to a part
of either city. Distance decay misses in two folds, once above and once below the prediction;
it rests on few pairs of ponds within half a city, so these misses may be noise, but they may
also mean that a single exponential kernel for both cities is too simple a description of
space.

## What this example shows

The workflow ran from a simulator to checks of the fit, and each step said something the
previous one could not. Recovery showed, before we looked at the data, that `lambda` cannot be
learned from them. Model choice preferred competition among close relatives with a probability
near one, and the posterior predictive checks and cross-validation then showed that this model
does not reproduce the phylogenetic structure of the ponds, and suggested where to look next: a
filter conserved in the phylogeny, or limits to colonisation from the region. An earlier
version of this analysis, with the pool of each city restricted to the species recorded there,
made the observed total richness the largest value a simulation could reach, and that bound
alone pushed the estimate of competition towards zero; the choice of the regional pool matters
as much as the choice of the model. The analysis is meant to illustrate the functions, not to
test hypotheses about these frogs, which would also need a model of detection if abundances were
used (see `observe_detection()`).
